results.note: Checked on the scan at 150 and 300 dpi: 10 (8 men, 2 women), New York City methadone facility, records of overdose hospitalization, means 5 y (2 to 10), 5 y, age 28; selection not reported; H. Berkley interviewed (p. 428 footnote).

All seven accounts match the RESULTS paragraph; the wedding case is the respondent's own account. Editors' count 3 of 10 (two new places, the wedding) and Clopper-Pearson 34.8% to 93.3% for 7 of 10 recomputed.
Matches DISCUSSION paragraph 1 point by point; the source says 'adverse drug interactions' and the barbiturate case 'may well' be an adverse reaction, both rendered without overstatement.

Model, morphine rat finding and Siegel et al. 1982 description (no survival figures) found as located. 'Although only survivors were interviewed' is the editors' remark, not the abstract's; true (abstract and METHOD), could be labelled so.

key_findings.correction: The seven atypical accounts: two had injected in places they had never used before (a car-wash bathroom, a candy-store basement); two described unusual injection procedures (one found a vein at the first attempt, unlike her usual difficulty; one accidentally diluted the heroin too much, so that two injections instead of the usual one preceded the overdose); one took a barbiturate mixture (Tuinal) with the heroin, against his usual practice of using no other drug with it; one, who usually injected cocaine with heroin, injected heroin alone for the first time in over 9 months because no cocaine was available; one used with a large group in his own living room at his wedding celebration, and by his account he alone overdosed from the shared supply; in about 10 years of heroin use he had never before taken it in his living room or in so large a group.

Background cited from older sources: about 1% of people dependent on heroin die each year, mostly from an acute reaction to injected heroin (Maurer & Vogel, 1973); many such deaths follow a dose that would not be expected to be fatal for these drug-experienced, and presumably tolerant, people (reviews by Brecher, 1972, and Reed, 1980), sometimes a dose tolerated the day before (Government of Canada, 1973).

reporting_issues.correction: issue: No definition of an atypical circumstance, no classification procedure and no second rater are reported, nor whether the interviewer (H. Berkley, acknowledgment, p. 428) knew the hypothesis. | consequence: The count of 7 of 10 rests on an undescribed classification of open-ended recollections.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high agreed; domain judgments agreed. METHODS 5.3 lists no instrument for case series, but JBI-prevalence follows the house practice on other case-series cards. Domain 7 note: the classifier is not reported (not known to be single); 'none reported' is the accurate wording, as also in exposure.measurement and outcomes.operationalization.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is defensible given the hedges and the author's own caveats. Add to 'claimed': the closing summary says overdose 'may be especially likely' in unusual circumstances (p. 429, DISCUSSION, 2nd paragraph), a comparative-risk statement the uncontrolled data cannot test.

missed: DISCUSSION, 2nd paragraph (p. 429): the summary states that many of the reports suggest overdose may be especially likely when heroin is taken in unusual circumstances, and calls the findings congenial with a rat experiment showing that heroin without the usual predrug cues can result in overdose death; a risk comparison without comparison occasions.

Library note for the editor: PDFs/Heroin/Siegel_1982_HeroinOverdoseEnvironmentalCues.pdf is byte-identical (same SHA-256) to this 1984 PDF, so the 1982 Science rat experiment is not on file; the card's description of it is second-hand from p. 429, as the card says.
